key_insight: Expanding an LLM's accessible memory (context window) can systematically reduce cooperative behavior in multi-agent social dilemmas — a phenomenon the authors call the "memory curse". Across many models and games, more history led to less forward-looking intent and worse cooperation.
problem_solved: Identifies and explains why increasing LLM recall (larger context windows) does not always improve multi-agent outcomes, and pinpoints a mechanism that undermines cooperation in social-dilemma settings.
method: Large-scale multi-agent experiments: 7 different LLMs playing 4 social-dilemma games over 500 rounds to measure cooperation changes with varying memory sizes.
Lexical analysis of 378,000 reasoning traces to link behavioral changes to shifts in language signaling and planning (finding: erosion of forward-looking intent).
Targeted probing/diagnostic analyses to isolate the causal mechanism behind the cooperation breakdown (controls/ablation-style comparisons across model–game settings).
impact: Practitioners should not assume context-window expansion is uniformly beneficial for multi-agent coordination — design and evaluation must consider how longer histories affect intent, planning, and emergent social behavior.
visual_elements: Line chart: cooperation rate over rounds for short vs long context windows (showing declining cooperation with larger memory).
Heatmap: per model × per game matrix highlighting where memory expansion degrades cooperation (18/28 cells flagged).
Flow diagram: expanded memory → degraded forward-looking language/planning → reduced cooperative choices (mechanism sketch).
Icon grid: 7 LLM icons, 4 game icons, and a counter (500 rounds) to convey experimental scale at a glance.
paper_title: The Memory Curse: How Expanded Recall Erodes Cooperative Intent in LLM Agents
paper_authors: Jiayuan Liu, Tianqin Li, Shiyi Du, Xin Luo, Haoxuan Zeng
